title: The Monsoon Ghazal
body:
The rains have come again, washing the dust from every stone, Mehta.
I wait at the window, counting drops like lost years, every stone.
My father's voice returns with thunder — do not forget where you began.
Even the river forgets its source, yet always returns to its stone.
Separation is the name we give to love we cannot hold, Mehta.
The rains have come again, washing the dust from every stone.

title: Neon Puddle
body:
Convenience store sign—
its reflection shivers
in the rain-drenched street

title: Praise Song for the Baobab
body:
You are older than the kingdom's first sorrow.
Your roots drink from rivers we have forgotten to name.
Beneath your canopy, the elders spoke in proverbs;
your bark remembers the hands of every season.
Do not tell me you are just a tree —
I have seen you hold an entire village's grief
in one night of harmattan.

title: Border Sonnet
body:
They ask me which side of the river I belong.
I say: both banks, and the current between.
My grandmother's tongue is a bridge I cross each dawn,
my mother's silence, the toll I pay at dusk.
There is a map inside my chest — its borders shift
each time I say a word in the language I was taught to forget.
I have drawn and redrawn the line: here, origin;
here, arrival; here, the long uncertain drift.
Do not ask me to choose one horizon only.
The eye holds east and west without apology.
I am the hyphen in the official form, the comma
between two countries that have never met.
Borders are fictions that bleed. I am the scar
and the healed skin both.

title: Ode to the Euphrates
body:
O Euphrates, keeper of the first alphabet,
your waters wrote the names of gods before gods had names.
I have walked your banks at dawn when the mist
turned the world back to clay — formless, waiting.
Every city you fed has fallen; you outlasted them all.
What is empire to a river? What is glory to water?
Flow on. Flow on. We are the temporary ones.

title: Algorithm Sijo
body:
The machine learns my face before I know my own reflection—
I type my grief in search bars; it sells me grief in return.
Who taught the river to only flow toward the advertised sea?

title: Elegy for a Leningrad Courtyard
body:
The courtyard remembers what the city has paved over:
a linden tree, its roots still splitting the stones.
We played there, Nina and I, the summer before everything.
Now Nina is in the ground. The linden is gone.
Only the stone remembers, and stone does not speak —
yet I come back each year to press my hand against it,
reading the cold the way a blind woman reads a face.

title: The River Does Not Forget
body:
They dammed the Niger in the name of progress;
the fish did not receive the memorandum.
We signed our names on papers we could not read,
and woke to find the river wearing new clothes.
But the river does not forget its old name —
it whispers it in flood season, every time,
reclaiming every field they thought they owned.
